chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn Hadeed, from Jameel, from Zurara, from one of the two Imams (peace be upon them), similar to it.

Humayd ibn Ziyad, from Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad Al-Kindi, from Ahmad ibn Al-Hasan Al-Mithamī, from Aban ibn Uthman, from Abu Al-Abbas, who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), 'A man guaranteed for a man the person of another man, saying, 'If you bring him to me, or else five hundred dirhams are upon you.' The Imam (peace be upon him) said: 'He is obligated to bring the person, and no dirhams are upon him.' Then he said, 'If he had said, 'Five hundred dirhams are upon me if I do not hand him over to you,' the Imam (peace be upon him) said: 'The dirhams would be obligated upon him if he did not hand him over to him.'

key_terms.بِنَفْسِ رَجُلٍ: for the person of a man (personal guarantee)
key_terms.كَفَلَ: to guarantee or take responsibility for

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between guaranteeing a person and guaranteeing a debt in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith, narrated by Imam al-Sadiq (AS), clarifies the fiqh of 'kafalah' (guarantee) by distinguishing between guaranteeing a person's presence and a monetary debt. The Imam establishes that unless the penalty is explicitly conditioned as a debt upon failure, the guarantor is not financially liable, emphasizing the principle of strict interpretation in contractual obligations. This ruling reflects the Shia scholarly emphasis on precise linguistic stipulations in civil transactions to avoid unjust enrichment.
